Preliminary treatment consists of barrel grinders followed by aerated grit removal.
Following preliminary treatment, wastewater is pumped into rectangular primary sedimentation basins to remove floatable and settleable material.

Primary effluent is gravity-fed to 440 acres of mechanically aerated Oxidation Ponds, where organic matter and ammonia are degraded by aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. Nitrification and denitrification in the ponds are linked to ambient weather conditions and experience seasonal variations.
Treated pond effluent is pumped to Fixed Growth Reactors (FGRs) (i.e., trickling filters) that provide additional nitrification of ammonia.

FGR effluent is conveyed to the Dissolved Air Flotation Tanks (DAFTs), where compressed air and polymer are injected to coagulate, flocculate, and remove biological solids (algae and bacteria) generated during treatment in the Oxidation Ponds and FGRs.
Following biological treatment, the wastewater undergoes filtration through four parallel dual media filters, two of which may be used to produce recycled water.

Sodium hypochlorite is metered into the filtered effluent at the beginning of four serpentine chlorine contact tanks to generate a chlorine residual (generally chloramines) for disinfection. As the effluent leaves the contact tanks, sodium bisulfite is added as needed to neutralize the hypochlorite.
The Discharger pumps sludge produced in the primary sedimentation basins to primary anaerobic digesters.

The Discharger pumps digested sludge (biosolids) to an equalization tank, conditions the biosolids with polymer, and mechanically dewaters them using a belt filter press to approximately 20 to 25 percent solids prior to land application or disposal at a landfill.

Secondary treatment solids removed by dredging the oxidation ponds are chemically conditioned in an equalization tank and dewatered using a centrifuge or belt filter press to approximately 20 to 25 percent solids prior to land application or disposal at a landfill.

On average, the Discharger treats about 5 to 10 percent of the wastewater the plant processes to meet Order No. 94–069 requirements for disinfected tertiary recycled water.

This project includes the phased design and construction of new headworks, primary sedimentation tanks, an influent pump station, grit removal facilities, and associated electrical, mechanical, and control systems... the new facilities would better protect downstream processes and improve biosolids quality through use of influent bar screens and high efficiency grit basins.

The Discharger proposes to replace the current biological treatment facilities with an activated sludge system consisting of bioreactors and secondary clarifiers configured as a Modified Ludzak-Ettinger (MLE) process to enhance nitrogen removal. First, the Discharger would construct two aeration basins, four secondary clarifiers, and associated appurtenances.

For the second stage, the Discharger proposes to complete the remaining portion of the activated sludge system and phase out the existing biological treatment system; however, operation of the Oxidation Ponds under a split-flow regime could continue, allowing the Discharger to retain flexibility in managing its flow due to the large storage capacity of the ponds.
